entries.clue: Make quite clear what to do at end of holiday? (5,4)

annotation.definition2: what to do at end of holiday?

blocks.note: to drive a point home is to make it unmistakable

blocks.clueFragment: what to do at end of holiday?
blocks.note: literally, the car journey back when the holiday is over

annotation.surface: A question about the last day of a trip away.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, literal reading: the idiom and the motorway journey are the same two words.
annotation.definitionFit: To drive something home is to press it until it is fully understood, which is making it quite clear.

entries.clue: Unaware about cold drink (5)

indicatorNotes.about: About means around, so the word for unaware is wrapped around the letter for cold.

blocks.note: deaf to something = unaware of it
C = cold, as on a tap

annotation.surface: Someone is oblivious to the chill of their drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deaf to' a warning is being unaware of it, which is how 'Unaware' reaches DEAF.
annotation.definitionFit: Decaf is short for decaffeinated coffee, a hot beverage with the caffeine removed.

entries.clue: I can’t stand up straight to deliver patter song (3,3,1,6,4)

blocks.note: to list is to lean, so a little list is a slight tilt
Ko-Ko's rapid-fire song in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado

annotation.surface: Someone who cannot stand straight is asked to perform a comic song.
annotation.walkthrough: A ship that lists leans to one side; read that way, the song title is a confession of a slight lean. A patter song is sung at speed with many words.
annotation.definitionFit: "I've Got a Little List" is the best-known patter song in The Mikado.

entries.clue: Delightful daughter missing: with prospect of being returned? (9)

indicatorNotes.missing: The daughter is missing: her letter is taken out.

blocks.note: D = daughter, and this is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A charming daughter has gone missing and might yet come home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returned' sounds like a lost child coming home; it is the British sense of being returned to Parliament at an election.
annotation.definitionFit: An electable candidate has a real prospect of being returned, that is, elected.

entries.clue: Beginning two terms of tennis (6)

blocks.note: 'out' is the call when a ball lands beyond the lines
a set is a unit of a tennis match

annotation.surface: The opening of a tennis lesson on its vocabulary.
annotation.walkthrough: The one phrase supplies both halves: OUT and SET are each a tennis term.
annotation.definitionFit: The outset is the point at which something sets out, its start or commencement.

entries.clue: Degas perhaps broken by conflict with key enigmatic man (6,5)

indicatorNotes.broken by: EDGAR is broken open and the other letters go into the gap.

blocks.note: Edgar Degas, the French painter, is one Edgar
the Delete key on a keyboard

annotation.surface: A painter's work is interrupted by a war.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Degas perhaps' asks for his first name, not the painter. The definition is a nod to Elgar's Enigma Variations.
annotation.definitionFit: Elgar composed the Enigma Variations, so he is the man behind the enigma.

entries.clue: Vegetables, with lots of people in line for them, we hear; mind them? (2,3,2)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer: P's and Q's are what you mind.

indicatorNotes.we hear: What we hear is sound, so the words are spelt differently from how they are said.

blocks.note: peas said aloud are the letters P's
queues of people, said aloud, are the letters Q's

annotation.surface: Crowds line up for vegetables at a market stall.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end as a question: 'mind your P's and Q's' means watch your manners.
annotation.definitionFit: The idiom is 'mind your P's and Q's', so P's and Q's are the things to mind.

entries.clue: Knights taking great care to protect youngster (8)

indicatorNotes.to protect: PAINS wraps round LAD as if protecting him.

annotation.surface: Knights take great care to guard a child.
annotation.walkthrough: Knights protecting the young is so natural a picture that the container hardly shows.
annotation.definitionFit: Paladins were Charlemagne's knights, and the word means any chivalrous knight.

entries.clue: A part of Ireland, removing large English grave (7)

indicatorNotes.removing: The large is removed: its letter L is taken out of ULSTER.

blocks.note: Ulster is the northern province of Ireland
L = large, as on clothing, and this is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A travel note about part of Ireland and a burial.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grave' at the end looks like a noun for a tomb; it is the adjective meaning solemn.
annotation.definitionFit: Grave and austere both mean severe and serious in manner.

entries.clue: Not truly attractive, one way the dawning of love must break in (11)

indicatorNotes.must break in: ONE, ST and L break into DISHY.
indicatorNotes.the dawning of: The dawning of love is its first letter, L.

blocks.note: the dawning, the first letter, of love

annotation.surface: Someone is only superficially attractive until love breaks through.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Love' usually gives O in crosswords; here only its first letter is wanted. Dishy is British slang for good-looking.
annotation.definitionFit: Dishonestly describes acting falsely or deceitfully, the opposite of truly.

entries.clue: Reckless with the cosmetics? (4-5)

blocks.note: careless in a cheerful, devil-may-care way
slap is British slang for make-up, so happy with the slap

annotation.surface: A question about someone careless with their make-up.
annotation.walkthrough: Slap is British slang for make-up; the question mark says the second reading is a joke: happy with slap.
annotation.definitionFit: Slap-happy describes a cheerfully careless, devil-may-care approach that ignores consequences.

entries.clue: Radiant with Russian girl returning (5)

indicatorNotes.returning: OLGA comes back, so it reads right to left.

blocks.note: Olga is a typical Russian girl's name

annotation.surface: A Russian girl comes home glowing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link between definition and wordplay; it is the W at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Aglow describes something shining with warm light, as a happy face shines.

entries.clue: Without leader, orchestra try to keep right tempo (7)

indicatorNotes.Without leader: A word without its leader has lost the letter that leads it, its first.
indicatorNotes.to keep: To keep something is to hold it, so the word for try holds the letter for right inside it.

blocks.note: the Hallé is the Manchester orchestra
have a go = have a try

annotation.surface: An orchestra without its leader tries to hold the right tempo.
annotation.walkthrough: The orchestra's leader is its principal violinist, which makes 'Without leader' read as players in trouble; it means lose the first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Allegro, Italian for lively, marks a brisk, quick musical speed.

entries.clue: Slept again, concealing some small old coins (5)

indicatorNotes.concealing some: The phrase conceals some of its letters: the answer runs across the words.

annotation.surface: Someone takes a second nap and hides a few coins.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition comes last, after the hiding phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Lepta (singular lepton) were small coins of ancient Greece, the widow's mites of the Bible.

entries.clue: Regular occasions when being married, say, ends in confusion (10)

indicatorNotes.in confusion: SAY ENDS is thrown into confusion, its letters jumbled.

annotation.surface: Someone reflects that married life ends in confusion.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas make 'say' look like 'for example'; it is fodder alongside 'ends'.
annotation.definitionFit: Wednesdays come round every week, so they are regular occasions.

entries.clue: Cold, simple chemical substance losing one electron at first becomes mild (7)

indicatorNotes.losing: Losing something means no longer having it, so the substance's word drops a letter.
indicatorNotes.at first: At first points to what comes first, so only the opening letter of electron is taken.

blocks.note: an element cannot be broken down chemically
the first letter of electron, which goes

annotation.surface: A chemistry lesson: an element loses an electron and turns mild.
annotation.walkthrough: The chemistry is all surface: an atom losing an electron is real science, but here only the letter E is lost.
annotation.definitionFit: Clement, from Latin clemens, describes gentle, merciful weather or temperament.

entries.clue: Cries aloud for the country (5)

indicatorNotes.aloud: Said aloud, WAILS sounds like the country.

annotation.surface: Someone cries out for their homeland.
annotation.walkthrough: The picture of a patriot weeping for the country is the disguise.
annotation.definitionFit: Wales is one of the four nations making up Britain, with Cardiff its capital.

entries.clue: Put name into small newspaper article, curving along the edges (9)

indicatorNotes.Put: Put says to place the name somewhere.
indicatorNotes.into: The name goes into the rest.

blocks.note: an op-ed is an opinion piece opposite the editorial page
to call someone something is to name them

annotation.surface: An editor adds a name to a short article.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Name' is a verb here, giving CALL, not the usual N.
annotation.definitionFit: A scalloped edge curves in a row of shell-like arcs.

entries.clue: Lifelong description of how “rock-a-bye-baby” fell to its death? (4,3,6,2,3,5)

annotation.answer: FROM THE CRADLE TO THE GRAVE
annotation.definition2: description of how “rock-a-bye-baby” fell to its death?

blocks.clueFragment: description of how “rock-a-bye-baby” fell to its death?
blocks.note: in the nursery rhyme the bough breaks and down falls the cradle

annotation.surface: A grim reading of the lullaby Rock-a-bye Baby.
annotation.walkthrough: The rhyme ends with the cradle falling; the question mark makes that fall literal, from cradle to grave.
annotation.definitionFit: From the cradle to the grave means throughout one's life.

entries.clue: Singular taxi-driver making a crust (6)

annotation.surface: A remarkable taxi-driver earns a living.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Making a crust' is British slang for earning a living, which suits a taxi-driver; here it means forming a scab.
annotation.definitionFit: A healing wound forms scabs, hard dried layers of blood, so a scabby one is crusting over.

entries.clue: Capital assembled in very short order (5)

indicatorNotes.short: The order is cut short: FIAT loses its last letter.

blocks.note: so = very, as in so good
a fiat is a decree or order

annotation.surface: A capital city was built very fast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In very short order' reads as one idiom for quickly; it splits into very, short and order.
annotation.definitionFit: Sofia is Bulgaria's largest city and the seat of its government.

entries.clue: This is me at college, before being covered in flour etc (8)

annotation.surface: A student describes getting covered in flour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This is me' reads like an introduction; it is simply ME. Meunière is a French cooking term.
annotation.definitionFit: Fish à la meunière is dredged in flour and fried in butter.

entries.clue: Reminder to collect protective gear held up (7)

blocks.note: a prod is a nudge or reminder

annotation.surface: Someone is reminded to fetch safety gear that has been delayed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Held up' looks like delayed, fitting the gear; it means supported.
annotation.definitionFit: Something propped rests on a prop, a support such as a pole or beam keeping it upright.

entries.clue: Importantly, no cops interfered with this publication (8,9)

indicatorNotes.interfered with: The letters are interfered with, jumbled.

annotation.surface: A book was published without the police interfering.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface nods to the book's notoriety: Philip Roth's frank novel was banned in some places.
annotation.definitionFit: Philip Roth's scandalous 1969 novel, narrated as a monologue to a psychiatrist, is the publication meant.

entries.clue: Chest: one heard having trouble with it? (6)

indicatorNotes.heard: A word that is heard reaches us as sound, so its spelling can differ from the answer's.

blocks.clueFragment: one heard having trouble with it
blocks.note: a cougher has trouble with the chest

annotation.surface: Someone with a chest complaint is overheard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chest' does double duty: the definition, and the 'it' the cougher has trouble with.
annotation.definitionFit: A coffer is a strongbox for money and valuables, the treasure chest of a household or state.

entries.clue: Figure Noah went swimming? Seems reasonable (4,6)

indicatorNotes.went swimming: Letters that swim move around freely.

annotation.surface: Noah taking a swim is a reasonable thing to imagine, given the flood.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Figure' looks like the start of a definition or a verb; it is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Fair enough is the conversational concession granting that an argument or request makes sense.

entries.clue: Almost attractive at first not before time (6,6)

indicatorNotes.at first: At first means the first letter of not: N.

annotation.surface: Something is nearly attractive, but only at first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At first' attaches to 'not', not to 'attractive'.
annotation.definitionFit: Pretty nearly is an informal phrase for very close to, all but, as in pretty nearly finished.

entries.clue: Country golf club welcoming wife (6)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: R AND A welcomes W inside.

blocks.note: the R and A, the Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews

annotation.surface: A country golf club welcomes a member's wife.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country golf club' reads as a single rural club; 'Country' is the definition. The R&A is golf's governing club at St Andrews.
annotation.definitionFit: Rwanda is a small landlocked nation in central Africa, capital Kigali.

entries.clue: Formerly holding name Max? (5)

indicatorNotes.holding: Holding means clasping something within, so the word for formerly holds the name's letter inside it.

annotation.surface: A question about someone formerly called Max.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks Max as a first name, not maximum: Max Ernst the surrealist.
annotation.definitionFit: Max Ernst was a German-French surrealist painter.

entries.clue: Illegally induce son, delivered by hairpin? (6)

annotation.surface: A son is delivered with the help of a hairpin, which sounds criminal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Delivered by hairpin' reads as the means of birth; BORN just sits beside U.
annotation.definitionFit: To suborn is to induce someone to commit perjury or another crime.

entries.clue: Like to hear detective who lived in Mexico (5)

indicatorNotes.to hear: Something given for us to hear arrives as sound, so the spelling may change on the way.

blocks.note: as = like; said aloud, the S buzzes like a Z

annotation.surface: A detective who once lived in Mexico.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a relative clause: an Aztec is one who lived in Mexico.
annotation.definitionFit: The Aztecs were the people who ruled central Mexico before the Spanish conquest.

entries.clue: Smart person wiping chlorine from part of fingernail (5)

indicatorNotes.wiping: Wiping the chlorine off removes CL.

blocks.note: the cuticle is the skin at the base of the nail
Cl is the symbol for chlorine, and these letters go

annotation.surface: A manicurist cleans chlorine from a fingernail.
annotation.walkthrough: Chlorine on a swimmer's nails makes the surface; Cl is the chemical symbol.
annotation.definitionFit: Besides a pretty girl, a cutie is a clever, cunning operator, someone too sharp to be fooled.

entries.clue: Recipe for astringent to be put on back (7)

indicatorNotes.to be put on back: The astringent is put back to front.

annotation.surface: A recipe for an ointment to put on the back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link joining 'Recipe' to what follows; it is the first three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A formula lists ingredients and method, as a chemist's or a baby-milk formula does.

entries.clue: Great desire of Yankee as a salaryman? (8)

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: The ambition of an American office worker.
annotation.walkthrough: Yankee is the radio code word for Y. A salaryman is a salaried office worker.
annotation.definitionFit: Yearning is an intense longing, the ache of wanting something badly.

entries.clue: A fine fabric, very red (6)

blocks.note: lamé is fabric woven with metallic thread

annotation.surface: A fine red fabric.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine fabric' reads as one phrase; fine is just F.
annotation.definitionFit: A face aflame is burning bright scarlet with blushing or anger.

entries.clue: O my! — missing from holy book is the nucleus (8)

indicatorNotes.missing from: O MY goes missing from the book's name.

blocks.note: Deuteronomy, fifth book of the Bible

annotation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at something missing from the Bible.
annotation.walkthrough: 'O my!' looks like an exclamation; it is the letters that come off the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A deuteron, one proton plus one neutron, is the nucleus of heavy hydrogen, deuterium.

entries.clue: Briefing about problem, my answer’s complicated (4,7)

indicatorNotes.about: The jumbled letters go about SUM.
indicatorNotes.complicated: MY ANSWER is complicated, its letters mixed.

blocks.note: a sum is a maths problem

annotation.surface: Someone admits their briefing on a problem got complicated.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's of 'answer's' is 'is', joining wordplay to the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A news summary gives the day's headlines in short form, which is what a briefing does.

entries.clue: Overdo it regularly with friend of a parricide (7)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Regularly means taking every other letter.

annotation.surface: Someone overdoes it with a friend who killed his father.
annotation.walkthrough: Oedipus killed his father, the parricide of the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Oedipal means relating to Oedipus, who killed his father.

entries.clue: Galley slave toiling through passages in literal pursuit? (11)

annotation.definition: Galley slave toiling through passages in literal pursuit?

blocks.clueFragment: toiling through passages in literal pursuit?
blocks.note: the passages are paragraphs of text, and a literal is a misprint being hunted down

annotation.surface: A slave rows a Roman galley.
annotation.walkthrough: Galleys are printer's proofs and a literal is a printing error, so the slave is a proofreader hunting typos.
annotation.definitionFit: A proofreader works through galley proofs looking for literals.

entries.clue: Loves meeting in the street? Go ahead (5)

blocks.note: have a go = have a try

annotation.surface: Lovers meet in the street and are urged on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loves' is the plural noun, lovers; a tryst is their meeting.
annotation.definitionFit: A tryst is a secret romantic rendezvous arranged between lovers.

entries.clue: Signal for bed, when eating a series of snacks (5)

indicatorNotes.when eating: TAPS eats A, taking it inside.

blocks.note: taps is the bugle call for lights out

annotation.surface: The bedtime bugle sounds while someone is eating.
annotation.walkthrough: Taps is the military bugle call for lights out.
annotation.definitionFit: Tapas are small Spanish dishes served one after another with drinks.

entries.clue: Commando in protected area out of line calling in engineers (5,5)

indicatorNotes.out of: The line is taken out of the area.
indicatorNotes.calling in: RE is called into the gap.

blocks.note: green belt is protected land around a town

annotation.surface: A commando in a guarded zone steps out of line and summons engineers.
annotation.walkthrough: Green belt is British planning land kept free of building. The military surface hides a town-planning term.
annotation.definitionFit: Green Berets are commandos, named for their headgear.

entries.clue: Create storm to find necessary cash (5,3,4)

annotation.surface: Someone creates a fuss to squeeze money out of people.
annotation.walkthrough: To raise the wind is an old British idiom for getting hold of money.
annotation.definitionFit: Raising the wind means getting the money you need.

entries.clue: Hospital people who are experienced get together affectionately (4,5)

annotation.surface: Experienced hospital staff meet warmly.
annotation.walkthrough: The split H + OLD HANDS is hidden by the answer's own break after HOLD.
annotation.definitionFit: Couples clasp each other's hands as a tender sign of closeness.

entries.clue: Tiny policeman is ineffective (3,4,3)

blocks.note: literally, not much of a cop

annotation.surface: A small policeman is no use.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not much cop' is British slang for not very good.
annotation.definitionFit: Not much cop is British slang for of little use or value; cop here is an old word for a catch or prize.

entries.clue: Very old Roman soldier? (9)

blocks.note: punning on centenarian, someone a hundred years old

annotation.surface: A question about an ancient Roman soldier.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark allows the pun: a centurion commands a hundred, as a centenarian lives a hundred years.
annotation.definitionFit: A centurion commanded a century, a unit of about eighty to a hundred legionaries.

entries.clue: A missing pet’s hard to catch, having fouled dishes (8)

indicatorNotes.to catch: To catch something is to trap it inside, so the lost pets close around the letter for hard.

blocks.note: a stray is a missing pet; the 's supplies the final S

annotation.surface: A lost pet is hard to catch after messing up the dishes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fouled' looks like part of the pet's crime; it describes the dishes, fouled with ash.
annotation.definitionFit: Ashtrays are dishes that smokers dirty with ash and cigarette stubs.

entries.clue: Loiters uncertainly in luxury resort (7)

indicatorNotes.uncertainly: Letters placed uncertainly are in no fixed order.

annotation.surface: Someone hangs around uncertainly in a smart resort.
annotation.walkthrough: Estoril is a resort on the Portuguese coast near Lisbon.
annotation.definitionFit: Estoril, on the coast west of Lisbon, is famed for its casino and glamorous hotels.

entries.clue: Sort of desk surface: light lunch on it? (4-3)

indicatorNotes.on it: The lunch goes on the surface, so ROLL comes first.

annotation.surface: Someone eats a light lunch at their desk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Desk surface' reads as one phrase; 'Sort of desk' is the definition and 'surface' gives TOP.
annotation.definitionFit: A roll-top desk has a sliding slatted cover.

entries.clue: Quietly leaves with order to remove underwear? (5,3)

blocks.note: to slip off is to leave unnoticed
petticoats are the underwear, and the command tells the wearer to shed them

annotation.surface: Someone slips away after being told to undress.
annotation.walkthrough: A slip is a woman's underskirt, so 'Slips off!' is an order to remove them.
annotation.definitionFit: To slip off is to depart unobtrusively, without anyone noticing you go.

entries.clue: Take apart one section of roof: nothing in it (7)

annotation.surface: A builder dismantles part of a roof and finds nothing in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take apart' reads as dismantle; it means set apart.
annotation.definitionFit: To isolate something is to separate it, setting it away from everything around it.

entries.clue: Hostility as I am surrounded by a group of students (6)

indicatorNotes.surrounded by: I AM is surrounded by NUS.

annotation.surface: Someone feels hostility on being surrounded by a student group.
annotation.walkthrough: The NUS is Britain's National Union of Students.
annotation.definitionFit: Animus, Latin for mind or spirit, has come to mean ill will or animosity.

entries.clue: Trap eccentric viewer (6)

blocks.note: a spider's web is a trap
an eccentric is a kind of cam in engineering

annotation.surface: A trap for an odd onlooker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like an anagram signal; in engineering an eccentric is a cam.
annotation.definitionFit: A webcam is a small internet camera that lets distant people watch.

entries.clue: Hate run-of-the-mill BBC type messing up patriotic song (6,4,2,3,8)

indicatorNotes.messing up: The letters are messed up, rearranged.

anagram.fodder: HATE RUN OF THE MILL BBC TYPE

annotation.surface: A dull broadcaster mangles an anthem.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end; 'Hate' at the start is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Julia Ward Howe's Civil War hymn, beginning 'Mine eyes have seen the glory', is sung as an American anthem.

entries.clue: Time on boat for rescuing a creature in river (5)

indicatorNotes.on: Time comes on, before, the boat.

annotation.surface: A boat sets out to rescue an animal from a river.
annotation.walkthrough: Tarka the Otter is Henry Williamson's river otter.
annotation.definitionFit: Tarka is the otter of Henry Williamson's novel, a creature of the river.

entries.clue: One might believe this Indian died (5)

blocks.note: the Cree are a Native American people

annotation.surface: A statement that a Native American died.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Indian' means a Native American people, the Cree.
annotation.definitionFit: A creed is a statement of faith, such as the Nicene Creed recited in church.

entries.clue: Universal train and air travel in the country one imagined (9)

annotation.surface: A traveller goes by train and plane through a make-believe land.
annotation.walkthrough: Universal is U, the British film rating for all ages. Ruritania is the invented kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda.
annotation.definitionFit: Ruritania is an imagined country from Anthony Hope's novels.

entries.clue: A minor honour (5)

blocks.note: a child under guardianship is the guardian's ward

annotation.surface: A small decoration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Minor honour' reads as a modest decoration; 'minor' is a young person, a ward.
annotation.definitionFit: An award is a prize or decoration given in recognition of achievement.

entries.clue: Cooking us one nice stew (7)

annotation.surface: A cook makes a nice stew for us.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stew' reads as the dish; it is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Cuisine is a style of food preparation, as in French or Thai cuisine.

entries.clue: Parking vehicle first, go for long walk (5)

indicatorNotes.first: The vehicle comes first, before P.

annotation.surface: Having parked the car, someone sets out on a hike.
annotation.walkthrough: Parking comes first in the clue but P goes last in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: To tramp is to trudge heavily over great distances, as hikers do.

entries.clue: In nervous state, throw coconut perhaps at head (7)

indicatorNotes.at: At places the head after the throw.

blocks.note: at a coconut shy you throw balls at coconuts

annotation.surface: A nervous fairground-goer throws at a coconut.
annotation.walkthrough: A coconut shy is a British fairground stall. 'At head' reads as aiming for the top; NESS is a head of land.
annotation.definitionFit: Shyness is timidity, the anxious unease some people feel around others.

entries.clue: Considered odd, having been eaten by a bear? (9)

blocks.note: something eaten is in the eater
a ted is a teddy bear

annotation.surface: Something odd is mused over after a bear eats it.
annotation.walkthrough: Rum is British for odd; a ted is a teddy bear.
annotation.definitionFit: To ruminate is literally to chew the cud, and figuratively to mull something over.
